item.text:
AMLO was still Mexico’s president in 2022. The legal frame is strong on paper but constrained in practice: the presidency holds the federal executive power, is single-person, six-year, and non-reelectable, yet it is checked by Congress, the courts, the electoral authorities, autonomous bodies, and a fragmented security environment. I did not use the client matrix, and I did not re-fetch the structured local-prior facts you already supplied.

**Retained source set**
- [Constitución Política de los Estados Unidos Mexicanos](https://www.diputados.gob.mx/LeyesBiblio/ref/cpeum.htm) | Cámara de Diputados | current text on site; relevant articles were in force in 2022 | Precise fact: the executive power is vested in one president; the term is six years with no re-election; the president can issue regulations and has defined constitutional powers, while courts and electoral institutions remain separate constraints. | Best for 1B, 4B, 7B | Ruler attribution is institutional, not personal; this is legal authority, not performance evidence. | Contrary points: the Constitution does not prove how much effective control AMLO had over Congress, courts, or agencies in 2022.

- [Versión estenográfica. 4° Informe de Gobierno](https://www.gob.mx/amlo/articulos/version-estenografica-4-informe-de-gobierno) | Presidencia de la República | 1 Sep 2022 | Precise fact: AMLO personally presented the fourth government report from Palacio Nacional and framed the administration around welfare, infrastructure, public health, education, austerity, Pemex, and CFE. | Best for 5B, 6B, 8B | Highly self-serving primary source; it shows what he claimed, not independent verification. | Contrary points: opposition and investigative coverage challenge several of the claimed achievements and policy effects.

- [Se presenta contexto de agravios hacia periodistas y personas defensoras de derechos humanos](https://www.gob.mx/segob/prensa/se-presenta-contexto-de-agravios-hacia-periodistas-y-personas-defensoras-de-derechos-humanos) | Secretaría de Gobernación | 8 Mar 2022 | Precise fact: the government itself acknowledged a context of journalist and human-rights abuses, citing organized crime, impunity, corruption, and collusion. | Best for 3B, 8B | Official framing; it is useful for baseline conditions but not for full accountability or ruler blame. | Contrary points: the government’s own anti-impunity narrative does not settle whether its response was adequate.

- [México: Ratifican a AMLO en consulta con poca participación](https://www.latimes.com/espanol/articulo/2022-04-10/mexico-ratifican-a-amlo-en-consulta-con-poca-participacion) | Los Angeles Times / Associated Press | 10 Apr 2022 | Precise fact: the recall vote backed AMLO by a large margin but fell far short of the participation threshold, so it had no binding legal effect. | Best for 4B, 8B | News-wire framing; it captures the institutional constraint, not a deep policy analysis. | Contrary points: supporters treated the result as political validation even though it was not legally binding.

- [Mexican president's contentious electricity overhaul defeated in Congress](https://www.stabroeknews.com/2022/04/18/news/regional/mexican-presidents-contentious-electricity-overhaul-defeated-in-congress/) | Reuters via Stabroek News | 18 Apr 2022 | Precise fact: AMLO’s constitutional electricity overhaul was defeated in the lower house; the bill would have expanded state control and reduced private-sector participation. | Best for 4B, 5B, 8B | Reuters syndicated copy; strong on event facts, lighter on domestic political texture. | Contrary points: AMLO still had already secured some policy movement through the earlier statutory electricity-law changes and later litio legislation.

- [La Suprema Corte avala la ley eléctrica de López Obrador](https://elpais.com/mexico/2022-04-07/la-suprema-corte-avala-la-ley-electrica-de-lopez-obrador.html) | EL PAÍS México | 7 Apr 2022 | Precise fact: Mexico’s Supreme Court upheld the 2021 electricity-law changes favorable to CFE, while litigation and amparos still limited implementation. | Best for 4B, 5B, 8B | Analysis-heavy, and it reflects a liberal/critical editorial posture. | Contrary points: the ruling was a partial legal victory for AMLO, even if implementation remained contested.

- [Con AMLO incrementan 85% los ataques contra la prensa: Artículo 19](https://animalpolitico.com/2022/04/amlo-incrementan-ataques-prensa-articulo-19) | Animal Político | 4 Apr 2022 | Precise fact: the Article 19 report said press attacks rose sharply under AMLO and tied the pattern to official rhetoric and the use of presidential briefings as a stigmatizing platform. | Best for 3B, 4B | Strongly critical and advocacy-linked; excellent for pressure/hostility, weaker for neutral balance. | Contrary points: the government argued it was combating misinformation and protecting honest journalists.

- [Mexico](https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk/digital-news-report/2022/mexico) | Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism | 15 Jun 2022 | Precise fact: the Mexican media environment was highly polarized, journalists continued to be murdered, and AMLO’s daily briefings were a major driver of hostility toward critical outlets. | Best for 3B, 4B | Secondary analysis, not a first-order event report. | Contrary points: it explains the media climate but does not by itself prove direct state responsibility for each abuse.

- [“Sí, cambié de opinión”: AMLO sobre el regreso del Ejército a los cuarteles](https://animalpolitico.com/2022/09/amlo-regreso-ejercito-cuarteles-cambie-opinion) | Animal Político | 6 Sep 2022 | Precise fact: AMLO publicly said he had changed his mind on returning the military to the barracks and wanted soldiers to remain in public-security roles beyond his original promise. | Best for 2B, 8B | Critical local-language reporting; strong on ruler attribution and security posture. | Contrary points: supporters frame this as adaptation to inherited violence, not ideological reversal.

- [Iniciativa de AMLO reconoce al litio como patrimonio de la nación](https://www.jornada.com.mx/noticia/2022/04/18/politica/iniciativa-de-amlo-reconoce-al-litio-como-patrimonio-de-la-nacion-1842) | La Jornada | 18 Apr 2022 | Precise fact: after the electricity defeat, AMLO pushed a litio law casting lithium as national patrimony and reserving exploration/exploitation to the state. | Best for 5B, 8B | Favorable/left-leaning domestic coverage; useful for the administration’s own framing. | Contrary points: critics saw it as a counterreform and a sign of policy volatility after legislative defeat.

- [Mexican government suffers major data hack, president's health issues revealed](https://www.investing.com/news/world-news/mexico-president-confirms-leak-of-government-data-admits-health-issues-2903047) | Reuters via Investing.com | 30 Sep 2022 | Precise fact: the military data breach exposed sensitive defense information, including AMLO’s health issues, and underscored how much security infrastructure had shifted into military hands. | Best for 2B, 7B, 8B | Syndicated Reuters copy; strong on exposure and vulnerability, weaker on deeper institutional context. | Contrary points: AMLO publicly acknowledged the hack, which limits uncertainty about whether the breach occurred.

**Office, authority, constraints**
- Office: president of Mexico, the single head of the federal executive.
- Authority: executive appointment/removal, regulations, foreign policy execution, agenda-setting, and substantial agenda control through the daily briefing system and presidency-centered communication.
- Constraints: no re-election, supermajority requirements for constitutional change, Congress’s ability to block reforms, Supreme Court review, autonomous electoral and oversight bodies, and a violent/security environment that limits governability.

**Major 2022 events**
- 10 Apr: recall referendum ratified AMLO politically but had no binding legal force.
- 7 Apr to 18 Apr: electricity-law victory at the Court, then constitutional-overhaul defeat in Congress.
- Apr onward: litio became the fallback policy banner after the energy setback.
- Feb to Sep: continuing conflict with media, attacks on journalists, and public stigmatization of critics.
- Aug to Sep: AMLO moved toward keeping the military in public-security roles beyond 2024.
- 30 Sep: military data hack exposed state vulnerability and details about his health.

**Inherited conditions**
- Entrenched organized violence and journalist killings.
- Weak rule of law and low trust in institutions.
- A divided legislature after the 2021 midterms.
- Legal and market conflict over energy policy inherited from the 2013 reform era.
- Severe pressure on media freedom and a polarized information environment.

**Compact event map**
- `Q1 2022`: press hostility, journalist killings, media conflict.
- `Q2 2022`: recall referendum, energy-law and electricity-reform battles, litio pivot.
- `Q3 2022`: military/security expansion, fourth government report, governance stress.
- `Q4 2022`: cyber-hack exposure, continued centralization of security and communication.

**Chapter source plan**
- `1B`: keep to the Constitution only unless a later source specifically links AMLO to nuclear-force policy.
- `2B`: use local UCDP/SIPRI facts plus the military-extension and hack sources if narrative attribution is needed.
- `3B`: use Segob, Animal Político, Reuters Institute, and the government’s own press posture for press-freedom context.
- `4B`: use the Constitution, recall referendum, and the electricity court/Congress sources for democratic and institutional constraints.
- `5B`: use the Fourth Report, La Jornada on litio, and the Reuters electricity-overhaul defeat for economic and policy direction.
- `6B`: rely mostly on the local HDI/health/education facts already supplied; the Fourth Report is enough for ruler framing.
- `7B`: use the Constitution plus the hack and media-climate sources for accountability and corruption-adjacent institutional weakness.
- `8B`: use the Fourth Report, military-extension coverage, the hack, and the energy sources for governing capacity and execution.
